title: Estimating Term Premiums in the Current Low-Rate Environment
abstract: A careful look at how term premiums behave when policy rates are low, and why the usual models may mislead.
body:
## Introduction

As a former central-bank economist, I have spent much of my career staring at yield curves and wondering how much of the compensation investors demand for holding long-term bonds is truly a term premium. In the current environment, where policy rates in many advanced economies remain low by historical standards, that question has become both more important and more difficult to answer. This newsletter is not a forecast; it is an attempt to think through the estimation challenges, separating what central banks have said from what markets have done.

Let me start with a definition. The term premium is the extra return investors expect to earn for holding a long-term bond instead of rolling over short-term instruments. It is not directly observable. We infer it from asset prices using models that embed assumptions about expectations, risk, and market structure. When rates are low and central bank balance sheets are large, those assumptions become strained.

## What the Models Assume

The workhorse models in this literature, from the affine term structure models to the more recent shadow-rate frameworks, typically assume that the short rate will eventually return to some long-run mean. They also assume that the central bank's policy rule is stable and that market participants form expectations rationally. In a low-rate environment, these assumptions are not obviously wrong, but they are harder to defend.

For instance, if the policy rate is near its effective lower bound, the distribution of future short rates is truncated. Standard models that ignore this truncation can produce biased estimates of the term premium. Researchers have tried to correct for this by using shadow-rate models, which allow the policy rate to go negative in a notional sense. But these models rely on the same expectations hypothesis that has been questioned in the literature.

Another issue is the role of quantitative easing. When a central bank buys long-term bonds, it compresses the term premium directly. Disentangling the effect of QE from other factors is notoriously difficult. The Bank of Japan, for example, has been a major buyer of Japanese government bonds for years. Its actions have likely pushed the term premium on JGBs to very low or even negative levels. But estimating exactly how low is a challenge.

## The Data Problem

Even if we had a perfect model, we would still face data limitations. In a low-rate world, the variation in short rates is small, which makes it hard to identify the parameters that govern expectations. Moreover, the yield curve itself may be less informative because of segmentation and regulatory changes. Pension funds and insurers, for example, have strong demand for long-duration bonds, which can depress term premiums independent of monetary policy.

I recall a conversation with a colleague at the Bank for International Settlements who argued that we should focus on survey-based measures of expectations rather than model-based ones. Surveys can be useful, but they are noisy and may not reflect the marginal investor's views. They also suffer from small sample sizes and potential strategic bias.

In practice, most analysts use a combination of models and market-based measures, such as the spread between forward rates and expected short rates. But even that spread is contaminated by liquidity premiums and other frictions. In the current environment, where many central banks hold large portfolios of government bonds, liquidity conditions are unusual.

## Recent Evidence

Let me turn to some recent evidence, though I must stress that these are estimates and subject to revision. In the United States, several widely followed models suggest that the term premium on 10-year Treasuries has been negative for much of the past decade. That is unusual. Negative term premiums imply that investors are willing to pay a premium for the safety and liquidity of long-term government bonds, rather than demanding compensation for duration risk.

In Japan, the situation is even more pronounced. The Bank of Japan's yield curve control policy, which caps 10-year JGB yields around zero, has effectively suppressed the term premium. Some estimates put it at negative 50 basis points or lower. But these estimates are model-dependent. If you use a different model, you might get a different answer.

The European Central Bank's experience is also instructive. After the ECB introduced negative policy rates and asset purchases, term premiums on German bunds fell sharply. They have since recovered somewhat, but remain low by historical standards. Again, the exact level is uncertain.

What does this mean for investors? If term premiums are negative, then long-term bonds are expensive relative to short-term ones. That could be a signal that markets expect weak growth and low inflation for a long time. Or it could be a sign that central bank purchases have distorted the market. Probably both.

## Implications for Policy and Markets

For central banks, the existence of negative term premiums complicates the transmission mechanism. If long-term rates are already low, further cuts in the policy rate may have less effect on borrowing costs. This is the so-called reversal rate argument. It is not universally accepted, but it is worth taking seriously.

For market participants, the key takeaway is that term premium estimates should be treated with caution. They are not precise measures. They are model-based constructs that depend on assumptions about expectations, risk, and market structure. In a low-rate environment, those assumptions are particularly fragile.

I would also note that the term premium is not a policy target. Central banks do not set it directly. They influence it through their policy rate and asset purchases. But they cannot control it precisely. This is an important distinction that is sometimes lost in public commentary.

Looking ahead, if inflation picks up and central banks normalize policy, term premiums may rise. But the path is uncertain. The COVID-19 pandemic has left scars on the global economy, and the recovery is uneven. Supply chain disruptions and labor market mismatches could keep inflation volatile. In that case, term premiums might remain low for longer than expected.

Alternatively, if inflation expectations become unanchored, term premiums could spike. That would be a painful adjustment for bondholders. But it is not my base case. I am not in the business of forecasting; I am in the business of understanding the uncertainties.

## Conclusion

Estimating term premiums in a low-rate environment is as much an art as a science. The models we use are approximations, and the data we have are imperfect. As an ex-central-bank economist, I have learned to be humble about such estimates. They are useful for thinking about risk and return, but they should not be treated as precise measures.

What I can say with more confidence is that the term premium is an important concept for understanding bond markets. It helps explain why long-term yields are where they are, and it informs how monetary policy transmits to the real economy. In the current environment, it is likely negative or very low in many advanced economies. But the exact number is elusive.

I will continue to watch the data and the models. And I will continue to separate what central banks say from what markets do. That is the only way to make sense of this complex landscape.
